titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State

div.head: 411. Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State
div.p: 1819. Subject: Ambassador Walters’ tête-à-tête with President Stroessner.

2. Background: The following is an account drafted by Ambassador Vernon Walters on his 15 minute tête-à-tête with President Stroessner on April 22. It followed his hour and 15 minute meeting with the President (reported septel), which also included Major General Johannsen, two of Ambassador Walters’ staff and Ambassador Taylor.
3. Begin text: President Stroessner said he had asked to speak to me alone for a few minutes because he could speak more frankly that way. I said I also had some things I could say to him.

4. President Stroessner said that he was very disturbed that U.S. Government officials had accused senior Paraguayan officials of being active in drug trafficking. He had asked for names and specifics. He had received none. If the U.S. was not prepared to furnish the names, then they should refrain from such public accusations. He said if we would give him names and locations, he would take action against the drug traffic, if necessary, using the army. He felt that traffic in narcotics was a threat to every nation. Bolivia was a producer. Paraguay was not. I said that there were recent indications of two large shipments to Europe having transited Paraguay. Again he asked for names, dates and places.

5. President Stroessner said that he felt that Embassies were for the purpose of improving relations. Sometimes he felt ours in Paraguay was not helping this. I replied that he must understand that our policies were determined in Washington, and the Ambassador, like me, received his instructions from our government. These instructions
were often the result of legislative action arising from a congressional perception of what was happening in Paraguay. If he wanted better treatment from us, he must help us to help him.

6. I said the Paraguayan people were grateful to him for the improvements in Paraguay and for stability and leadership he had provided. He could easily open things up in the area of the media. A hostile speech on the radio or a hostile article in the press were no threat to him, and would certainly improve the image of his country in the U.S. and in Congress. I said he was strong enough to allow some opposition. He replied that communists and others were trying to destabilize Paraguay and that was not in our interest. I said that I agreed but that a little more flexibility in allowing freedom of expression would help.

7. I said another matter that helped give him a bad image abroad was the matter of political prisoners who had taken asylum in foreign embassies in Asuncion, and who were not allowed to leave the country. President Stroessner said that they were not political prisoners, but criminals. However he had decided to let them leave the country. He said the Argentines, who disliked his government, were willing to take them, and they would be allowed to leave the country “in a matter of days.” I told him that this was a wise move (I had previously reminded him that in 1976 he had released another political prisoner, Chase Sardi, at my request).

8. President Stroessner said that the present Argentine Government had armed, trained and sent agents across the border to stir up guerrilla activity in Paraguay. This had failed because guerrillas needed popular support and they had obtained none in Paraguay. He then attacked Argentina and Alfonsin for their hostility toward Paraguay.

9. Finally, he said that he appreciated the chance to speak frankly to me and the fact that I would speak frankly to him. He hoped I would remember what he had told me, and he would think over the things I had told him. End text.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880765–0007. Secret; Immediate; Exdis. Sent for information to USUN and Buenos Aires.

In telegram 113881 to USUN and Asuncion, April 12, Abrams wrote to Walters about his April 22–23 trip to Paraguay, warning him “that Stroessner’s request that he receive you and Ambassador Taylor together briefly, but then would expect Clyde to withdraw so that he could have a separate private meeting with you is an obvious ploy that would undercut the Ambassador and create the appearance of a division between a senior representative of the administration and the Ambassador.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880746–0203)

In telegram 1841 from Asuncion, April 26, the Embassy reported on Walters’ and Taylor’s April 22 meeting with Stroessner. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880358–0705) In telegram 1862 from Asuncion, April 27, the Embassy provided an overview of Walter’s April 22–23 visit to Paraguay, noting that Walters had “underscored our support for democracy and our commitment to fight narcotics trafficking.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880362–0156)

In telegram 297181 to Asuncion, September 23, 1987, the Department reported on Abrams’ September 22, 1987, meeting at the UN General Assembly with Saldívar, who “claimed that recent repressive acts by the Paraguayan Government were necessary because conciliation would have been mistaken by the opposition as weakness and thus have led to chaos.” In reply, “Abrams stressed US concern that GOP’s acts would polarize society, and, almost inevitably, lead to radical violence. The future course and how the world would judge events in Paraguay can still be affected by the decisions of the GOP.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D870785–0833)

In telegram 2712 from Asuncion, July 1, 1976, the Embassy reported the “release of Professor Miguel Chase Sardi.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D760255–0283)
